title: I want to try using Opus for my next project, after using Astra almost exclusively. But I burn through tokens whenever I so much as glance at Claude. How can I use it efficiently?
author: CelestialButterflies
selftext:
I am finishing up my first vibecoded game, which is very exciting, I've never gotten this far in a project before. It's in Closed Beta on the Google play store while I finish up the last touches. (I still need more testers so it can go live, if anyone is interested, lol - it's a kanji drawing game, for the weebs out there).

While doing this, I'm simultaneously thinking about and planning my next game. It's going to be far more complex than my kanji game. Basically a city builder / management / board game with a winning condition, beatable in like 2 hours. That's the plan, anyway.

My process for the kanji game had been to give Codex a big chunk of clear directions for the next mechanic, and then test, ask it to fix some things, repeat. My prompts could be one task, or many. It completes everything relatively quickly and I can keep going for the whole month. I only this month upgraded from $20 to $100 because I ramped up my usage trying to finish this game.  

The process works but my kanji game was very simple. It's 2D, menu-based, with only one big mechanic, that granted took a lot of tweaking. But my next game won't be so easy.

I'm tempted to make it 3D, which I've never worked with before. And I think Opus might be a stronger fit for my complex vision? At least based off what I've seen people do with it. But - maybe I'm doing something terribly wrong. I tried switching to Claude (Sonnet High) for some simple tasks, gave it the same directions I'd give to Astra, and it took like 30 minutes and half my credits. Not only that, but there were a ton of errors in the debugger (Godot), and it broke the GUI. Meanwhile Astra actually opens up the game to take temp screenshots to "see" the game, and fixes things as they appear, before telling me it's finished.

(That said, brainstorming the game in Sonnet has been such a pleasant experience compared to brainstorming in ChatGPT).

I haven't tried Opus yet because I'm afraid of eating up my credits in an hour.

Can anyone share their secrets on how to use Opus efficiently? Thanks!!

comments.author: Wheelydope
comments.body: This may be obvious for most, but create handoffs and new chats for every system you want to work on. Having Claude read through all of the context in a long chat after hours and hours of work will burn credits extremely fast. This also allows you to adjust reasoning on every task to ensure you’re not wasting credits on easy tasks.

replies.author: CelestialButterflies
replies.body: That's interesting, and I'm probably dumb asking, but how do you create handoffs? Manually? Which is totally fine, I'm cool with manually, just curious. That's kind of what I've been doing too. New chat for every system. I have a "refactor mode" where we periodically update a script index to make it easier for ai to find what it needs. But I don't typically do a handoff. Maybe I should start!

replies.author: Professional_Yam1339
replies.body: Ask it to create a wrapping session skill that concludes the current session and the crafts a handoff prompt for you to seamlessly continue the work in a new session. Thats the simple explanation.

replies.author: Phoelectrix
replies.body: This is self promotion but I have developed a system that I think is better than most things out there. I use markdown files in obsidian based on a novel architecture that treats (and visualises) folder structures as branching “corals”. Every folder becomes a branch with subfolders becoming child branches and notes becoming leaves on those branches. As I work with an agent it is instructed to save prompts and summaries of the responses as notes which grow out the branches. At the end of a session it then rolls up summaries of the work achieved up the structure as makes sense. New instances then orient very efficiently off these summaries getting the right context depending on where in the coral (folder tree) you direct them. The plugin is called Liefwork, is free to use and can be installed in Obsidian via the community plugin store.

replies.author: Cubey42
replies.body: Not really, it worse, leaves things summarized. Better to offload the context into documentation it can brush up on if it needs

comments.author: StarMonkeyGames
comments.body:
I build my games semi automatically. And my $20 subscription on OpenAI is more than enough to cruise through development. I just build in chunks and create my own project system. 

You don't need Codex/WorkMode all the time either. And like knowing the architecture will definitely help you in the long run. Like I know how much work some feature would actually take. I know if the AI got lost. Or when it's gaslighting me. 

The regular chat window is more than enough to work on a class/function level. 

I've tried having agents do it all, but like they burn through tokens and alignment is a constant issue. It's like stress/pressure trying to reign them in all the time. And I found that I should just step into the code like a human traffic controller.

comments.author: Charming_You_25
comments.body: Use opus. 5.5 is the most cost efficient workhorse on the market for long running big codebase work.

comments.author: roach01gt
comments.body: I made a switch recently to have Opus 5.5 being the main director who I brainstorm with and have it write the tickets. Then I hand it off to Sol 6.1 for implementation. I have $20 Claude + $100 Codex. Working great so far and I much prefer Claude’s creativity.

replies.author: CelestialButterflies
replies.body: that's great, probably what I'm looking for! I also have the same subscription setup. Claude has been sooo nice to brainstorm with, I agree it's much more creative. What do you mean by write the tickets? The prompts to send to Codex?

replies.author: roach01gt
replies.body:
Yes so, let’s say I find a bug in the game. I report to Claude the issue. Claude then will hypothesize the likely cause, and write an issue ticket (it’s just a formal mark down) that states the bug, likely cause, describes tests to run to find the bug, and then after fixing the bug to run tests to make sure it’s corrected and didn’t introduce new bugs. It of course writes all that in a very technical way. 

Then i switch over to codex and say implement ticket T-016. When it is done, i let Claude know and it double checks before having me check.

comments.author: Old-Wolverine-4134
comments.body: I was thinking the same thing, but (for now), Opus 5.5 is giving me a lot more than expected. Weekly usage lasted exactly one week to the hour. I did extensive tasks, big game with multiple levels, all 3d assets, environment, game mechanics. And I have zero experience, so a lot of stuff was wasting tokens until I get what I wanted. And this with $100 sub. With the bigger one I imagine you can do wonders.

comments.author: frogic
comments.body: I can't seem to hit my limit with a max 20 plan.  At work I'm using sol 6.1 a LOT and might be the heavy lifter you want (or sonnette 5.5 if you're doing claude but its cache reads are like twice as expensive).  You can also do a lot of work with luna 6 but its VERY slow.

comments.author: Several-Mess2288
comments.body:
I’m working on two games. The first one, where I didn’t use a [`CLAUDE.md`](http://CLAUDE.md) file and relied on large, vague prompts like “make a game,” consumed the same number of tokens in just one day as the second game, which I worked on for six days.

For the second game, I followed a more structured approach: breaking the work into smaller steps, using `/clear` between different tasks, Sonnet for simpler tasks, and Opus for planning and more complex ones.

Both projects ended up consuming roughly the same number of tokens, but the structured approach allowed me to spread that usage over six days instead of burning through it in a single day.
